comparison: Perfect agreement on behavioral validation (C21-C23). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers affirm the task validation, reliability, and construct validity findings with strong statistical support. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Strong agreement on the key multivariate cuneus finding (C6, C20, C44-C45, C52-C53). Both evaluations recognize this as compelling evidence for compensation. OpenEval emphasizes the MVB boost analysis as the strongest evidence, while peer reviewers describe it as 'compelling evidence for task-specific compensatory activity.'

Complete agreement on RSFA vascular control (C35-C39, C88). Both evaluations support this methodological contribution. OpenEval describes it as strengthening overall findings, while Reviewer 3 specifically praised it as a 'laudable aspect' of the study.

Agreement on univariate ROI identification (C4, C28-C30). Both evaluations support the identification of frontal and cuneal regions using established criteria. OpenEval notes uncertainty about the cuneal interaction not surviving correction (C33), while peer reviewers affirm the overall univariate findings without raising this concern.

Partial overlap on univariate patterns (C31-C34). OpenEval rates these as UNCERTAIN due to the marginal cuneal interaction (p=0.028) not surviving correction, while peer reviewers accept the differential patterns between regions as part of the overall supported findings.

Agreement on negative frontal MVB findings (C46, C80). Both evaluations support the absence of age effects in frontal MVB boost analysis, distinguishing it from the cuneus. This negative finding is important for the overall interpretation.

Agreement on frontal spread analysis (C48-C49, C81). Both evaluations accept these negative findings. OpenEval notes the boost analysis is more compelling than spread (C50, C143), while peer reviewers implicitly endorse this through acceptance of the multivariate approach.

Strong agreement on main conclusions (C7, C53, C101). Both evaluations strongly support the interpretive claims about compensation in the cuneus. OpenEval emphasizes convergence of evidence and appropriate qualifications, while all peer reviewers explicitly endorsed these conclusions as 'well supported by the data.'

Agreement on synthesis of findings (C103). Both evaluations support the contrasting patterns between cuneus (compensation) and frontal regions (inefficiency). Peer reviewers implicitly endorsed this through acceptance of main conclusions.

Agreement on frontal inefficiency interpretation (C79, C82, C85, C100). Both evaluations support the conclusion that frontal findings reflect inefficiency rather than compensation. OpenEval provides detailed reasoning, while peer reviewers accepted this as part of the overall pattern.

Agreement on methodological insights (C93-C96). Both evaluations support the value of multivariate methods. OpenEval notes convergence across methods and MVB's unique contribution, while peer reviewers praised the multivariate approach as demonstrating effects that would be missed by univariate analysis.

Agreement on participant characteristics and sample quality (C104-C105). Both evaluations affirm the appropriateness of the sample. OpenEval describes methods as appropriate, while peer reviewers praised 'the large sample with a wide and even age distribution' and 'appropriate, rigorous methods.'

OpenEval evaluated standard univariate fMRI findings and MDN definition (C24-C27) as SUPPORTED with appropriate citations. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found, though these provide context accepted by reviewers.

OpenEval evaluated MVB quality control procedures (C42-C43, C138-C139) as SUPPORTED with appropriate exclusion criteria. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found, though methods were generally endorsed.

OpenEval rated functional interpretations of cuneal compensation (C55-C60) as UNCERTAIN due to speculative nature and acknowledgment that no explanation fully accounts for all results. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval rated explanations for negative constant term (C64-C69) as UNCERTAIN, noting logical inconsistencies and authors' acknowledgment that no explanation is fully satisfactory. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval evaluated alternative vascular and SNR explanations (C70-C76) as UNCERTAIN, noting design limitations but concluding these alternatives are not strongly supported. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found, though vascular controls were praised separately.

OpenEval evaluated fMRI acquisition and preprocessing (C114-C117) as SUPPORTED with standard, appropriate methods. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found, though overall methods were endorsed.

OpenEval evaluated ROI definition approach (C118-C121) as SUPPORTED, noting some circularity for univariate tests but independence of multivariate tests. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found, though whole-brain approach was praised.

OpenEval evaluated MVB method description (C122-C129) as SUPPORTED with appropriate implementation and citations. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found, though multivariate approach was endorsed.

OpenEval evaluated boost analysis methodology (C130-C137) as SUPPORTED with well-justified thresholds and appropriate categorical recoding. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found, though results were accepted.
OpenEval evaluated spread measure description and comparison to boost (C141-C143) as SUPPORTED, noting boost analysis is more compelling. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval evaluated statistical methods (C144-C147) as SUPPORTED with rigorous and well-justified approaches including standardization, covariates, and correction methods. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found, though rigorous methods were praised.

Peer reviewers praised methodological strengths including large sample size, wide age range, whole-brain approach, and rigorous methods (C3, C15-C18). OpenEval addressed these elements across multiple results (R17 for participants, R2 for whole-brain approach) but no single OpenEval result covers all these methodological praise points together.
